questions.prompt: The Euclidean distance from a point \(x\) to the hyperplane \(w^T x + b = 0\) is
options: \(\lvert w^T x + b\rvert / \lVert w\rVert\)
\(\lvert w^T x + b\rvert\)
\(\lVert w\rVert\)
questions.explanation: The numerator is the absolute residual of the hyperplane equation. Dividing by the norm of \(w\) converts that residual into a Euclidean length. Without the division the number scales when \((w, b)\) is scaled, even though the hyperplane does not move. The norm alone ignores the point. The raw dot product \(w^T x\) ignores both the offset \(b\) and the scaling.

questions.prompt: The hyperplane is \(2 y - 2 = 0\) in the plane, so \(w = (0, 2)\) and \(b = -2\). What is the distance from the point \((5, 4)\)?
questions.explanation: The absolute residual is \(\lvert 0 \cdot 5 + 2 \cdot 4 - 2\rvert = 6\). The norm of \(w\) is \(2\). The distance is \(6/2 = 3\). Reporting \(6\) forgets the normalization. Reporting \(2\) gives the norm. Reporting \(4\) gives a coordinate. The same distance is the geometric margin of a point whose signed residual equals \(6\) and whose weight vector has length \(2\).

questions.prompt: Normalizing so that the smallest functional margin equals \(1\) turns maximum-margin separation into
options: maximize \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) with no constraints
minimize \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) subject to \(y_i(w^T x_i + b) \ge 1\)
an unconstrained linear program in \(w\)
minimize \(\lVert w\rVert\) subject only to correct signs \(y_i(w^T x_i + b) \ge 0\)
questions.explanation: After scaling, every point satisfies \(y_i(w^T x_i + b) \ge 1\), and the geometric margin is \(1/\lVert w\rVert\). Maximizing that margin is minimizing \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\). A constraint that only asks for the correct sign allows \(\lVert w\rVert\) to approach zero and the margin formula to blow up. Maximizing the squared norm runs the wrong way. The objective is quadratic, so the program is not linear, and it is constrained.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that turns maximum-margin separation into a quadratic program. Each step uses the previous result.
questions.explanation: The signed distances are the quantities whose minimum is the margin, so they come first. The optimization is that minimum. Scaling uses the freedom to multiply \((w, b)\) by a positive number, which does not change the hyperplane, and it freezes the functional margin at \(1\). Only then is the margin equal to \(1/\lVert w\rVert\), and minimizing the square of the norm is the quadratic program. Minimizing the norm before the normalization still has a scale freedom.

steps: Write each correctly signed distance as \(y_i(w^T x_i + b)/\lVert w\rVert\).
Maximize the smallest of those distances.
Scale \((w, b)\) so the smallest functional margin \(y_i(w^T x_i + b)\) equals \(1\).
The problem is then: minimize \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) subject to those normalized inequalities.

questions.prompt: The normalized problem minimizes \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) subject to \(y_i(w^T x_i + b) \ge 1\). Which claims hold? The unknowns are \((w, b)\).
options: The objective is quadratic in the unknowns.
Every constraint is linear in the unknowns.
The Hessian of the objective is positive semidefinite.
The problem is a linear program.
The bias \(b\) appears in the quadratic objective.
questions.explanation:
The objective depends on \(w\) through a square, and each constraint is a linear inequality in \((w, b)\).
• The Hessian is the identity on the \(w\)-block and zero on \(b\), which is positive semidefinite, so the program is a convex quadratic program.
• A linear program would need a linear objective.
• The bias is absent from \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\). It appears only in the constraints.

questions.prompt: The squared distance from the point \((x, y)\) to the line \(p x + q y + r = 0\) equals
questions.explanation: The distance is the absolute residual divided by the norm of \((p, q)\). Squaring it removes the absolute value and gives \((p x + q y + r)^2 / (p^2 + q^2)\). Every name is used. On the declared ranges the denominator is positive and the value is positive. Omitting the square leaves a signed quantity. Omitting the denominator leaves the square of the residual, which scales if the line equation is multiplied through by a constant.

questions.prompt: A note rescales a separator whose functional margin on a point is \(4\) and whose weight vector has length \(2\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The geometric margin is the functional margin divided by the norm, so the first value is \(2\). Dividing \((w, b)\) by \(4\) divides both the functional margin and the norm by \(4\). The new norm is \(1/2\), and the new geometric margin is \(1 / (1/2) = 2\). Scaling does not change it. The false step reports the new norm as if it were the margin.

questions.figure_alt: One arrow leaves the origin in the plane.
steps: The geometric margin of this point is \(4/2 = 2\).
Dividing \((w, b)\) by \(4\) makes the functional margin equal to \(1\).
After that scaling, the new norm of \(w\) is \(2/4 = 1/2\).
reasons: Scaling \((w, b)\) leaves the geometric margin unchanged. The new value is \(1/(1/2) = 2\).
The original geometric margin is \(4\), not \(2\).

questions.prompt: In one dimension, separate the labeled points \((x, y_{\mathrm{label}}) = (3, +1)\) and \((1, -1)\) by minimizing \(\tfrac12 w^2\) subject to \(y(wx + b) \ge 1\). What is the optimal bias \(b\)?
questions.explanation: The two inequalities are \(3w + b \ge 1\) and \(-w - b \ge 1\). Adding them gives \(2w \ge 2\), so \(w \ge 1\). The objective wants the smallest nonnegative square, hence \(w = 1\). Then \(b = 1 - 3w = -2\), and the second inequality holds with equality as well. Reporting \(1\) gives \(w\). Reporting \(2\) drops the sign of the bias. Reporting \(1/2\) is the optimal objective \(\tfrac12 w^2\). The separating point is \(x = 2\).

questions.prompt: The normalized hard-margin problem, minimize \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) subject to the linear inequalities \(y_i(w^T x_i + b) \ge 1\), is
options: a linear program
a nonconvex program, because \(\lVert w\rVert^2\) is nonconvex
an unconstrained problem
a convex quadratic program
questions.explanation: The objective is a convex quadratic, since its Hessian is positive semidefinite, and the constraints are affine. That is a convex quadratic program. A linear program would have a linear objective. The squared norm is convex, not nonconvex. The inequalities are present, so the problem is constrained. Convexity is what makes a local solution a global one.

questions.prompt: At a hard-margin solution, a point that lies strictly beyond the margin has multiplier zero on its inequality, while a point on the margin may have a positive multiplier. That split is
options: complementary slackness
an equality multiplier, free in sign
a requirement that the Hessian be zero
a proof that the feasible set is empty
questions.explanation: Each inequality is \(1 - y_i(w^T x_i + b) \le 0\). Complementary slackness sets the multiplier times that residual to zero. A strict inequality, a point beyond the margin, forces the multiplier to vanish. A point on the margin may carry a positive multiplier. These constraints are inequalities, so the multiplier is not a free equality multiplier. The Hessian of the objective is not zero, and a solution is a feasible point.

questions.prompt: With \(w = (3, 4)\) and \(b = 10\), what is the distance from the point \((2, 1)\) to the hyperplane \(w^T x + b = 0\)?
questions.explanation: The absolute residual is \(\lvert 6 + 4 + 10\rvert = 20\). The norm of \(w\) is \(5\). The distance is \(20/5 = 4\). Reporting \(20\) forgets the division. Reporting \(5\) gives the norm. Reporting \(10\) gives the offset. The same quotient is the geometric margin of a correctly signed point with this residual and this weight vector.

questions.prompt: Two separators classify the same points. After both are normalized so the functional margin is \(1\), the quadratic program prefers
options: the larger \(\lVert w\rVert\)
whichever separator has a quadratic constraint
neither, because both programs are linear programs
the smaller \(\lVert w\rVert\), which is the larger geometric margin
questions.explanation: Under the normalization, the geometric margin is \(1/\lVert w\rVert\). Minimizing \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) therefore selects the larger margin. The larger norm is the smaller margin. The constraints of this program are linear. The quadratic piece is the objective. Neither program is a linear program.
